rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the clause about little knowledge cannot attach to the preceding examples; he notes a proposed reading as deliberate non-disclosure and a prohibition on further questioning.
rows.anchor: لا يمكن تعلقه بأمثال ذلك وهذا على ما قيل ترك للبيان ونهي لهم عن السؤال

rows.speaker: عطاء بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari report from Ata that the verse was revealed in Mecca; after the Hijra Jewish scholars asked whether its warning addressed them or Muslims, and the Prophet said both.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء بن يسار قال : نزلت هذه الآية بمكة فلما هاجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the same report, the Prophet explains that the Torah's religious guidance is little beside God's limitless knowledge, though useful when followed; this rejects a literally universal reading of its contents.
rows.anchor: هي في علم الله تعالى قليل وقد آتاكم الله تعالى ما إن عملتم به انتفعتم

rows.speaker: اليهود
rows.claim: A report authenticated by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Hakim says Jews called their Torah great knowledge and its possession a great good, prompting the verse about the sea.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية النسائي وابن حبان والترمذي والحاكم وصححاها أن اليهود قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports do not conflict: knowledge is relatively little beside God's knowledge and relatively abundant beside something below it.
rows.anchor: فالشيء يكون قليلا بالنسبة إلى ما فوقه وكثيرا بالنسبة إلى ما تحته

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Mardawayh reports that Jews claimed the address was theirs; the Prophet answered that it included both communities, and they contrasted it with the promise of abundant good through wisdom.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم لما قال ذلك قال اليهود : نحن مختصون بهذا الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast between abundant wisdom and little knowledge is also relative: human wisdom comprises what human capacity can grasp for worldly and afterlife order, little beside God's knowledge.
rows.anchor: الحكمة الإنسانية أن يعلم من الخير ما تسعه القوة البشرية

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj takes the address about limited knowledge as universal, applying to all people.
rows.anchor: وإلى تعميم الخطاب بحيث يشمل الناس أجمعين ذهب ابن جريج

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود والأعمش
rows.claim: Their reading وما أوتوا, together with the report explicitly addressing the questioners, points instead to a restricted audience; al-Iraqi calls the latter report unsound and Al-Alusi is unsure about the first report's status.
rows.anchor: ظاهر قراءة ابن مسعود والأعمش ( وما أوتوا ) فإنه يقتضي الإختصاص بالسائلين

rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: They explain the spirit as an originating creation brought into being by God's creative command كن, without material or derivation from another source; the answer gives a summary rather than the essence.
rows.anchor: معنى كون الروح من أمره تعالى أنه من الإبداعيات الكائنة بالأمر التكويني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concise answer redirects an inquiry into the spirit's essence: it is originated without matter, beyond human comprehension, and only this general description fits the stated limit of knowledge.
rows.anchor: فالمراد من الأمر واحد الأوامر أعني كن والسؤال عن الحقيقة والجواب إجمالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi compares this wise redirection to Moses answering Pharaoh's question about the Lord of the worlds, since the divine reality exceeds human apprehension.
rows.anchor: كجواب موسى عليه السلام سؤال فرعون إياه ما رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The little knowledge humans receive is largely gained through the senses, since abstract reasoning usually begins from sensed particulars; absent, imperceptible, or obscured things and their essences escape this route.
rows.anchor: علما قليلا تستفيدونه من طرق الحواس فإن تعقل المعارف النظرية إنما هو في الأكثر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some hold that the spirit's essence cannot be known, making the two proposed answers effectively alike.
rows.anchor: ظاهر كلام بعضهم أن الوقوف على كنه الروح غير ممكن

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafaji distinguishes the spirit, whose essence may be known, from the divine essence, which cannot be known.
rows.anchor: وفرق الخفاجي بأن بيان كنه الروح ممكن بخلاف كنه الذات الأقدس

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf says the spirit is known by removing veils from the heart's sight through the jewels of divine speech: clear to mystics, hidden from those occupied with other concerns.
rows.anchor: سبيل معرفة الروح إزالة الغشاء عن أبصار القلوب باجتلاء كحل الجواهر

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن بريدة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits his statement that the Prophet died without knowing the spirit; Al-Alusi suggests Ibn Burayda may have meant its knowledge is impossible.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن بريدة قال : لقد قبض النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وما يعلم الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi argues that otherwise the Prophet would not have died before learning everything knowable, citing the report of Muadh's night vision and disclosure of all things.
rows.anchor: فلم يقبض رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حتى علم كل شيء يمكن العلم به

rows.speaker: معاذ
rows.claim: A report from Muadh, called sound by al-Tirmidhi and hasan-sahih by al-Bukhari, describes God placing His hand between the Prophet's shoulders, after which everything became clear to him.
rows.anchor: عن معاذ رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال : إني قمت من الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some books vocalize the vision report with رأيت in the passive and الروح nominative; that reading weakens the objection but is less apparent.
rows.anchor: و ( رأيت ) يعلم في الخبر السابق في بعض الكتب مضبوطا بالبناء للمفعول والروح مضبوطا بالرفع

rows.speaker: بعض متأخري الصوفية
rows.claim: Some later Sufis say the spirit's essence, and indeed the essences of all things, cannot be grasped; Al-Alusi leaves acceptance or rejection to the reader.
rows.anchor: أنه يمتنع الوقوف على حقيقة الروح بل ذكر هذا البعض أن حقيقة جميع الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi questions treating command and creation as established Arab categories for immaterial and material things, and says the appeal to the verse about creation and command is weak.
rows.anchor: إطلاق عالم الأمر على الكائن من غير تحصل من مادة وتولد من أصل

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the question could concern many things, but the answer fits either the spirit's essence or whether it is eternal or originated.
rows.anchor: ليس في قوله تعالى : ( ويسألونك عن الروح ) ما يدل على وجه منها إلا أن الجواب المذكور

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: On the essence reading, the spirit is a simple, immaterial, originated substance whose effect is to give life to the body; ignorance of its specific essence does not negate its existence.
rows.anchor: أنها جوهر بسيط مجرد محدث بأمر الله تعالى وتكوينه وتأثيره إفادة الحياة للجسد

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: On the origination reading, the spirit is created by God; its initially empty state and later acquisition of knowledge would signal change and therefore origination.
rows.anchor: الأرواح في مبدأ الفطرة تكون خالية عن العلوم والمعارف ثم يحصل فيها ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi finds the origination argument a poor fit: the questioners could already know what they asked, so their limited knowledge does not suit this proof.
rows.anchor: لا يساعده التعرض لبيان قلة علمهم فإن ما سألوا عنه مما يفي به علمهم حينئذ

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Razi appears to distinguish disagreement about the human being's essence from disagreement about the spirit, though Al-Alusi is uncertain about that distinction.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كلام الإمام أن الاختلاف في حقيقته غير الاختلاف في حقيقة الروح

rows.speaker: جمهور المتكلمين
rows.claim: Most theologians identify the human being with the perceptible bodily structure; Al-Razi refutes this with seventeen transmitted and rational arguments.
rows.anchor: فذهب جمهور المتكلمين إلى أنه عبارة عن هذه البنية المحسوسة والهيكل المجسم المحسوس

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues that bodily parts change through growth, decline, and loss while the person is necessarily understood to persist through life.
rows.anchor: أجزاء البنية متغيرة زيادة ونقصانا وذبولا ونموا والعلم الضروري قاض بأن الإنسان

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Even when attention is absorbed by some or all bodily parts, a person remains aware of the self and says I acted or left something undone; the self is therefore not those parts.
rows.anchor: ولا يغفل عن نفسه المعينة بدليل أنه يقول مع ذلك الشاغل فعلت وتركت

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: The human essence can appear without its usual body, as with Gabriel in Dihya's form, or persist after its form changes, as in metamorphosis into an ape.
rows.anchor: جبريل عليه السلام كثيرا ما رؤي في صورة دحية الكلب وإبليس عليه اللعنة رؤي

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: A report says the deceased person's spirit flutters above the bier and warns family not to be deceived by worldly life or wealth, implying the human is something beyond the carried body.
rows.anchor: أن الميت إذا حمل على النعش رفرف روحه فوق النعش ويقول : يا أهلي ويا ولدي

rows.speaker: أقوال مختلفة
rows.claim: Other definitions identify the human as a spirit in the heart, an indivisible brain-part, innate heat from fiery elements, or blood; the source says nearly a thousand views exist.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن الانسان هو الروح الذي في القلب وقيل إنه جزء لا يتجزأ في الدماغ

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: One of two positions favored by investigators defines the human as a luminous, upper-world body distinct in essence from the perceptible body, permeating it and supplying life while it can receive its influence.
rows.anchor: جسم نوراني علوي حي متحرك مخالف بالماهية لهذا الجسم المحسوس

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi calls this corporeal-spirit position strong and noble because it closely matches scriptural accounts of life and death.
rows.anchor: مذهب قوي وقول شريف يحب التأمل فيه فإنه شديد المطابقة لما ورد في الكتب الإلهية

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim calls this position correct and the only sound one, claiming support from scripture, Sunna, the Companions' consensus, reason, innate disposition, and 105 proofs.
rows.anchor: إنه الصواب ولا يصح غيره وعليه دل الكتاب والسنة وإجماع الصحابة

rows.speaker: أكثر الإلهيين من الفلاسفة
rows.claim: A second position says the spirit is neither body nor bodily, inside nor outside the world, connected nor separate; it relates to the body by governing and acting upon it.
rows.anchor: أنه ليس بجسم ولا جسماني وهو الروح وليس بداخل العالم ولا خارجه

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم الراغب الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Al-Raghib, al-Ghazali, Ma'mar, al-Mufid, some Karramiyya, and most mystics and ascetics are listed among Muslim proponents of the immaterial-spirit view.
rows.anchor: منهم الشيخ أبو القاسم الراغب الأصفهاني وحجة الإسلام أبو حامد الغزالي

rows.speaker: ابن سينا
rows.claim: Ibn Sina wrote a separate treatise defending this view; Al-Alusi particularly commends its argument from the soul's awareness of itself.
rows.anchor: وللشيخ الرئيس رسالة مفردة في ذلك سماها بالحجج الغر أحكمها وأتقنها

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim refutes the arguments for an immaterial spirit in his beneficial book al-Ruh.
rows.anchor: وابن القيم زيف حججه في كتابه

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues from the verse that a bodily spirit would require an account of its material stages; the answer instead says it enters existence by God's creative command, indicating a holy immaterial substance.
rows.anchor: فلما لم يقل ذلك وقال هو من أمر ربي بمعنى أنه لا يحدث ولا يدخل في الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi calls this and similar scriptural or hadith arguments rhetorical persuasion rather than decisive proof; the spirit's divine attribution and related texts indicate its nobility and detachment.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أن ذلك من الاقناعيات الخطابية وهي كثيرة في هذا الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other suggestive proofs include the Prophet's descriptions as the naked warner and as one fed and sustained by his Lord, which imply spiritual distinction and nearness.
rows.anchor: أنا النذير العريان ففيه إلى تجرد الروح عن علائق الأجرام

rows.speaker: ثابت بن قرة
rows.claim: Thabit ibn Qurra says the spirit is attached to subtle, luminous celestial bodies that permeate the human body and govern it while present; Al-Alusi calls this a composite view but does not rule it out.
rows.anchor: ن قرة يقول : إن الروح متعلق بأجسام سماوية نورانية لطيفة

rows.speaker: المسلمون
rows.claim: Muslims agree the spirit is temporally originated like the rest of the world, but differ on whether it predates the body or arises afterward.
rows.anchor: أجمع المسلمون على أنه حادث حدوثا زمانيا كسائر أجزاء العالم إلا أنهم اختلفوا

rows.speaker: محمد بن نصر المروزي
rows.claim: A group including al-Marwazi and Ibn Hazm holds that spirits were created before bodies; Al-Alusi says Ibn Hazm falsely claims consensus for this view.
rows.anchor: فذهب طائفة إلى الحدوث قبل منهم محمد بن نصر المروري وأبو محمد بن حزم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: The sound hadith in both Sahih collections says spirits are gathered troops: those that recognize one another become harmonious and those that do not remain at odds.
rows.anchor: بما في الصحيحين من حديث عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : الأرواح جنود مجندة

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi interprets the hadith of spirits as evidence that souls were created before bodies; Ibn Hazm imagines them in a separate barzakh, descending to prepared bodies and returning after death, without scriptural proof.
rows.anchor: قال أبو سليمان الخطابي معنى هذا الحديث الإخبار عن كون الأرواح مخلوقة قبل الأجساد

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Some cite a report that God created spirits two thousand years before bodies, but Ibn al-Qayyim says its chain is unsound.
rows.anchor: خبر خلق الله تعالى الأرواح قبل الأجساد بألفي عام وتعقبه ابن القيم بأنه لا يصح إسناده

rows.speaker: حجة الإسلام الغزالي
rows.claim: Others, including al-Ghazali, hold that the spirit is created after the body begins forming; Ibn al-Qayyim cites the authentic fetal-development report in which an angel breathes in the spirit.
rows.anchor: وذهب آخرون منهم حجة الإسلام الغزالي إلى الحدوث بعد ومن أدلة ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim argues that if the spirit already existed, the report would say the angel brings it and inserts it, rather than breathing it into the fetus.
rows.anchor: أن الروح لو كان مخلوقا قبل لقيل ثم يرسل إليه الملك بالروح

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: In Rawdat al-Muhibbin, Ibn al-Qayyim calls pre-created spirits a plainly false view and says spirit and body are created together when the angel breathes into the fetus after four months.
rows.anchor: القول بأن الأرواح خلقت قبل الأجساد قول فاسد وخطأ صريح والقول الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says there is room for reflection on Ibn al-Qayyim's claim, while the verse about forming humans as another creation supports origination.
rows.anchor: انتهى وفيه تأمل ويوافق مذهب الحدوث قوله تعالى : ( ثم أنشأناه خلقا آخر )

rows.speaker: أفلاطون
rows.claim: Plato and earlier philosophers held the spirit eternal; Aristotle instead held it arises with the body's preparedness, as some Muslim thinkers did.
rows.anchor: وذهب أفلاطون ومن تقدمه الفلاسفة إلى قدم الروح وذهب المعلم الأول إلى حدوثها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers explaining that the body's particular temperament calls for a governing principle, and the Giver bestows an immaterial cognizer; the soul is immaterial in essence but dependent on the body in action.
rows.anchor: فالنفس الإنسانية مجردة ذاتا مادية فعلا فهي من حيث الفعل من التدبير والتحريك

rows.speaker: بعض صدور المتأخرين
rows.claim: A later eminent scholar suggests that Plato's statements about the soul's eternity can be given a subtle interpretation.
rows.anchor: ويمكن تأويل ما نقل عن أفلاطون في باب قدم النفس إلى هذا بوجه لطيف

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says most scholars treat spirit and soul as one thing, and reports use each term for the other.
rows.anchor: فحكى ابن زيد عن أكثر العلماء أنهما شيء واحد فقد صح في الأخبار إطلاق كل منهما على الآخر

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A sound raised report from Abu Hurayra describes a believer wishing for the soul to leave at death and the believer's spirit ascending to heaven, supporting the terms' interchangeability.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رفعه أن المؤمن ينزل به الموت ويعاين ما يعاين يود لو خرجت نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن حبيب
rows.claim: Ibn Habib distinguishes them: spirit is the breath moving in a person, while the soul has limbs and feels pleasure, pain, joy, and grief; it leaves during sleep and returns to the living body.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن حبيب : هما شيئان فالروح هو النفس المتردد في الإنسان والنفس أمر غير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن منده
rows.claim: Ibn Mandah transmits views that the soul is earthy-fiery and spirit luminous, or that the soul is human while spirit is divine; hadith scholars also distinguish them, with spirit sustaining the soul.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن منده عن بعضهم أن النفس طينية نارية والروح نورية روحانية

rows.speaker: أهل الأثر
rows.claim: The hadith scholars' distinction makes the soul the human form, desire, and trial, drawn to this world, while the spirit calls toward and prefers the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن أهل الأثر على المغايرة وأن قوام النفس بالروح والنفس صورة العبد

rows.speaker: المحقق الفرغاني
rows.claim: Al-Farghani defines the soul as a life-bearing vapor from the inner heart, shaped by the spiritual spirit, which governs the body and can incline toward either higher or lower qualities.
rows.anchor: أن النفس المضافة إلى الإنسان عبارة عن بخار ضبابي منبعث من باطن القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi's conclusion is that spirit and soul may be identical in some uses and distinct in others.
rows.anchor: والحق أنهما قد يتحدان إطلاقا وقد يتغيران

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim follows the majority in treating spirit and soul as one in essence; Sufis say the soul, after discipline and remembrance, becomes spirit and can rise to God's secret.
rows.anchor: وابن القيم اعتمد ما عليه الأكثرون من الاتحاد ذاتا

rows.speaker: الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufis describe four stages of ascent: purifying outward practice, cleansing inward character, adorning the soul with sacred forms, and effacing self-awareness before divine majesty.
rows.anchor: الأولى تهذيب الظاهر باستعمال النواميس الإلهية من القيام والصيام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seeker begins animal-like, gradually acquiring appetite, anger, greed, and envy; awakening to higher pleasures leads to repentance, turning to God, and leaving worldly excess for afterlife perfection.
rows.anchor: أن الإنسان أول ما يولد فهو كباقي الحيوانات لا يعرف إلا الأكل والشرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On entering the path, the seeker renounces distractions, adopts piety and true asceticism, and continually audits and distrusts the self because it loves desires and hidden snares.
rows.anchor: ثم إذا دخل في الطريق يزهد عن كل ما يعوقه عن مقصوده

rows.speaker: بعض الأكابر
rows.claim: An unnamed spiritual elder realized that his soul urged jihad only to escape the toil of prayer and fasting through death, so he refused its suggestion.
rows.anchor: يحكى عن بعض الأكابر أن نفسه لم تزل تأمره بالجهاد وتحثه عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As the seeker is purified, inner illumination reveals unseen flashes and imaginal realities, drawing him to retreat, remembrance, worship, watchfulness, and freedom from sensory pleasures.
rows.anchor: يتنور باطنه ويظهر له لوامح أنوار الغيب وينفتح له باب الملكوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seeker becomes absorbed in longing and ecstasy, witnesses hidden realities through unveiling, and eventually gains stable spiritual tranquility and visions of angels and higher realms.
rows.anchor: فيتحقق بالمشاهدة والمعاينة والمكاشفة ويظهر له أنوار حقيقية تارة وتختفي أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At annihilation, the seeker's sense of self collapses before divine majesty; remaining absorbed in unity veils him from creation, while a higher station returns him to sobriety and sees detail within unity.
rows.anchor: وهذا مقام الفناء والمحو وهو غاية السفر الأول للسالكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The returned knower sees God in everything and everything through God without multiplicity or corporeality, in a state beyond ordinary reason.
rows.anchor: ويرى كل شيء بالحق على وجه لا يوجب التكثر والتجسم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some describe the knower as truly assuming God's attributes; Al-Alusi rejects any idea that divine attributes become accidents in a human soul and allows only an ineffable relation beyond bodily qualities.
rows.anchor: لا بمعنى صيرورة صفاته تعالى عرضا قائما بالنفس فإن هذا مما لا يتصور أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sufi station described as becoming a secret of God may refer to this highest state, but it requires the path of the righteous, not speculation alone.
rows.anchor: ولعل مرادهم بالمرتبة التي تترقى إليها النفس فتكون سرا من أسرار الله تعالى

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: One group says the spirit dies because every soul tastes death, only God remains, angels also die, and the two deaths in the afterlife verse require death of both body and spirit.
rows.anchor: لأنها نفس وكل نفس ذائقة الموت وقد دل الكتاب على أنه لا يبقى إلا الله

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: Another group says the spirit does not die, since its reward or punishment continues after separation from the body until God restores it.
rows.anchor: إنها لا تموت للأحاديث الدالة على نعيمها وعذابها بعد المفارقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi defines the spirit's death as separation from the body; it tastes death in that sense but is not annihilated, returning for everlasting reward or punishment.
rows.anchor: موت الروح هو مفارقتها الجسد فإن أريد بموتها هذا القدر فهي ذائقة الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spirit is excepted from the trumpet's shock; shock need not mean death, and destruction can mean loss of function rather than annihilation; he rejects the proposed reading of the two deaths.
rows.anchor: وهي مستثناة ممن يصعق عند النفخ في الصور على أن الصعق لا يلزم منه الموت

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: Philosophers also say the soul survives bodily death, and Ibn Sina begins an argument that body and soul have no necessary causal dependence.
rows.anchor: وإلى أنها لا تموت بموت البدن ذهبت الفلاسفة أيضا

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: The philosophical proof says that if body and soul coexist without dependence, losing one need not destroy the other; if one depends on the other, neither can be the other's necessary cause.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت المعية في الوجود فقط من غير أن يكون لأحدهما حاجة في ذلك الوجود إلى الآخر

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: The body cannot cause the immaterial soul: corporeal causes act through position, matter is weaker than an immaterial substance, and the body is neither its receptive, formal, nor final cause.
rows.anchor: كل ما لا يفعل إلا بواسطة الوضع استحال أن يفعل أفعالا مجردة عن الحيز والوضع

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: Since body and soul have no necessary relation, the body's destruction from poor temperament, composition, or disintegration does not entail the soul's destruction.
rows.anchor: فإذا ليس بين البدن والنفس علاقة واجبة الثبوت أصلا فلا يكون عدم أحدهما علة لعدم الآخر

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: In reply to the objection that the body causes the soul's beginning, philosophers say a condition may trigger origination without being needed for continued existence, so its loss cannot cause the soul's destruction.
rows.anchor: كان شرطا للحدوث فقط وكان غنيا في وجوده عن ذلك الشيء

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: The body is an instrument through which the naturally perfection-seeking soul gains completion and governance; losing that instrument does not destroy the soul.
rows.anchor: ذلك الشرط مستعدا لأن يكون آلة للنفس في تحصيل الكمالات

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: Philosophers prove the soul's impossibility of annihilation, while Al-Alusi says that from his own theological position its annihilation is not impossible.
rows.anchor: ذهب الفلاسفة إلى استحالة انعدام النفس وبرهنوا على ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim says each soul takes an image from its former body and is more distinguishable from other souls than bodies are; he doubts individuation on the immaterialist account.
rows.anchor: أن كل روح تأخذ من بدنها صورة تتميز بها عن غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi disagrees that immaterial spirits cannot be distinguished: immaterialists can explain their differences by bodily attachment or another mode of individuation.
rows.anchor: فإن القائلين بذلك قائلون بالتمايز أيضا باعتبار ما يحصل لها من التعلق بالبدن

rows.speaker: إبراهيم الكوراني
rows.claim: Al-Kurani says departed spirits attach to fitting imaginal bodies, as suggested by reports that martyrs' spirits dwell in green birds and believers' children in sparrows.
rows.anchor: أن الأرواح بعد مفارقتها أبدانها المخصوصة تتعلق بأبدان أخر مثالية

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Sahih Muslim reports from Ibn Masud that martyrs' spirits dwell in the bellies of green birds; related reports describe them as green or white birds and children of believers as sparrows.
rows.anchor: في صحيح مسلم عن ابن مسعود أن أرواح الشهداء في أجواف طير خضر

rows.speaker: بعض المتكلمين
rows.claim: Some theologians reject reports placing spirits inside birds because two spirits cannot occupy one body; Al-Alusi says the objection overlooks that the bird could have only the martyr's spirit.
rows.anchor: لما في ذلك من تعلق روحين في بدن واحد وقد قالوا باستحالته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the reports mean a spirit is literally inside a bird, Al-Alusi says no impossibility follows, just as a fetus is inside its mother's body.
rows.anchor: لجواز أن تكون الروح في جوف الطير على نحو كون الجنين في بطن أمه

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: Reports indicate that spirits have different abodes after death: prophets are in the highest Illiyyin, martyrs in Paradise, and children's spirits are described similarly.
rows.anchor: الذي دلت عليه الأخبار أن مستقر الأرواح بعد المفارقة مختلف

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet's last words were a prayer for the highest companion, supporting the claim that prophets' spirits dwell in the highest Illiyyin.
rows.anchor: وصح أن آخر كلمة تكلم بها صلى الله عليه وسلم اللهم الرفيق الأعلى

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak transmits Ka'b's account of martyrs' souls grazing as green birds by a river at Paradise's gate under a green dome, receiving food morning and evening; Ibn Rajab assigns this perhaps to ordinary or afterlife martyrs.
rows.anchor: جنة فيها طير خضر ترعى فيها أرواح الشهداء على بارق نهر بباب الجنة

rows.speaker: الإمام الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i says ordinary believers' spirits also reside in Paradise, supported by the report that a believer's soul is like a bird in its trees until resurrection and by Umm Bishr's report.
rows.anchor: وأما مستقر أرواح سائر المؤمنين فقيل في الجنة أيضا وهو نص الإمام الشافعي

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says a white house in the seventh heaven is where the spirits of believers gather.
rows.anchor: إن لله تعالى في السماء السابعة دار يقال لها البيضاء يجتمع فيها أرواح المؤمنين

rows.speaker: أم بشر
rows.claim: A report from Umm Bishr places unbelievers' spirits in black birds' crops, eating and drinking fire and dwelling in Hell, where they plead not to be joined by their brothers.
rows.anchor: أن أرواح الكفار في حواصل طير سود تأكل من النار وتشرب من النار

rows.speaker: عامة أهل الحديث
rows.claim: Ibn Hazm attributes to most hadith scholars the view that the dead spirits reside in the courtyards of their graves, citing the displayed seat and the greeting to the inhabitants of believing graves.
rows.anchor: وقيل : مستقر أواح الموتى أفنية قبورهم وحكى هذا ابن حزم عن عامة أهل الحديث

rows.speaker: ابن عبد البر
rows.claim: Ibn Abd al-Barr prefers grave courtyards as the abode of spirits other than martyrs; Al-Alusi rejects permanent confinement there but accepts that spirits may be present temporarily.
rows.anchor: ورجح ابن عبد البر أن مستقر أرواح ما عدا الشهداء بأفنية القبور

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says spirits are above their graves for seven days after burial; Al-Alusi accepts this as temporary presence, not proof that the grave courtyard is their permanent abode.
rows.anchor: كما روي عن مجاهد الأرواح على القبور سبعة أيام من يوم دفن الميت

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some investigators say a spirit has an unknowable connection wherever it is, allowing it to return greetings, recognize visitors, and be shown its future seat.
rows.anchor: أن الأرواح حيث كانت لها اتصال لا يعلم حقيقته إلا الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others allow spirits to move from their abode and return rapidly wherever God wills.
rows.anchor: لامانع من انتقالها من مستقرها وعودها إليه في أسرع وقت

rows.speaker: ابن رجب
rows.claim: The Bara ibn Azib report says a believer's spirit is returned to the earth after its record is written in Illiyyin; Ibn Rajab says this alone cannot outweigh many reports placing spirits in Paradise, and the cited earth verse concerns bodies.
rows.anchor: إن حديث البراء وحده لا يعارض الأحاديث الكثيرة المصرحة بأن الأرواح في الجنة

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: A group places all spirits in the lowest heaven, to Adam's right or left, based on the Mi'raj report of people on either side whom he greets as destined for Paradise or Hell.
rows.anchor: مستقر الأرواح مطلقا في السماء الدنيا عن يمين آدم عليه السلام وعن شماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says seeing the two groups beside Adam does not prove their permanent abode is there; the Prophet saw Paradise and Hell from other locations too.
rows.anchor: فقد رأى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الجنة والنار في صلاة الكسوف وهو في الأرض

rows.speaker: النسفي
rows.claim: Al-Nasafi divides spirits into four abodes: prophets in Paradise, martyrs in green birds, obedient believers looking at Paradise, and sinful believers in the air between heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: جعل الأرواح على أربعة أقسام أرواح الأنبياء عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: النسفي
rows.claim: Al-Nasafi places unbelievers' spirits in black birds in Sijjin beneath the seventh earth, still connected to bodies so both spirit and body suffer.
rows.anchor: وأما أرواح الكفار ففي سجين في جوف طير سود تحت الأرض السابعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says al-Nasafi's claim that obedient believers do not enjoy Paradise conflicts with sound reports that their spirits do enjoy it.
rows.anchor: وما ذكره في أرواح المطيعين مخالف لما صح من أنها تتمتع في الجنة

rows.speaker: الإفصاح
rows.claim: Al-Ifsah reconciles reports by assigning blessed spirits varied forms and roles: in trees or birds, in Paradise forms, visiting their bodies, meeting new spirits, or under Adam's or Abraham's care.
rows.anchor: أن المنعم من الأرواح على جهات مختلفة منها ما هو طائر في شجر الجنة

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi calls this a good synthesis that reconciles reports, and al-Suyuti accepts it.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول حسن يجمع الأخبار حتى لا تتدافع وارتضاه الجلال السيوطي

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report reaching Malik says the spirit is released to go wherever it wishes; Al-Alusi says that, if sound, it cannot be unrestricted.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي الدنيا عن مالك قال : بلغني أن الروح مرسلة تذهب حيث شاءت

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some claim the spirit's abode is sheer nonexistence because it is an accident identified with life; Al-Alusi condemns this as false and contrary to revelation, consensus, and sound reason.
rows.anchor: حتى زعم بعضهم أن مستقرها لعدم المحض وهو مبني على أنها من الإعراض

rows.speaker: ابن برجان
rows.claim: Ibn Barjan distinguishes the soul, formed from the body's hidden essence, from spirit, formed from the soul's hidden essence; spirit's life is God's gift and its death is stillness, while bodily death is spirit's departure.
rows.anchor: والنفس مبرأة من باطن ما خلق منه الجسم وأوجد تبارك وتعالى الروح

rows.speaker: ابن برجان
rows.claim: For a believer, heaven opens and the spirit rises, while the soul's reality inhabits the lower region and the spiritual reality the heavens; this explains Moses praying in his grave and Abraham beneath a tree before ascent.
rows.anchor: فإن كان مؤمنا فتحت له أبواب السماء حتى يصعد إلى ربه عز وجل

rows.speaker: ابن برجان
rows.claim: For an evildoer, heaven does not open and the soul is cast down; Al-Alusi says this distinction resolves many apparent conflicts about spirit, soul, and bodily location.
rows.anchor: وإن كان شقيا لم يفتح له فرمي من علو إلى الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that a person recognizes a believing brother who passes his grave does not prove the spirit sits at the grave; the entity there may be the soul connected to spirit.
rows.anchor: ليس نصا في أن الروح على القبر إذ يفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spirits pass through states known only to God, including absorption in witnessing divine beauty; the hadith about the Prophet's spirit being returned means he awakens from that absorption to answer greetings.
rows.anchor: والذي ينبغي أن يعول عليه مع ما ذكر أن الأرواح وإن اختلف مستقرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though spirits have different reward-given abodes, they may roam God's kingdom by permission according to their nearness; some appear to living people while awake, and spirits meet, visit, and converse.
rows.anchor: لكن لها جولانا في ملك الله تعالى حيث شاء جل جلاله ولا يكون إلا بعد الإذن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Living and dead spirits may meet in dreams; only those who dismiss dreams as baseless fantasies deny this, but no legal ruling should rest on a dream because its truth remains uncertain.
rows.anchor: ولا يمكن ذلك إلا من يجعل الرؤيا خيالات لا أصل لها

rows.speaker: ثابت بن قيس بن شماس
rows.claim: In a report accepted as sound by Ibn Abd al-Barr and others, the slain Thabit appeared in a soldier's dream, identified his stolen armor and location, and requested payment of debts and emancipation of a slave.
rows.anchor: وكان عليه درع نفيسة فمر به رجل من المسلمين فأخذها فبينا رجل من الجند نائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi explains that Abu Bakr's execution of Thabit's testament was allowed by his daughter as heir because circumstances supported the dream; alternatively, payment came from public funds.
rows.anchor: بأن ذلك كان بإجازة الوارث وهي بنته لغلبة ظن صدق الرؤيا

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim records similar, even more remarkable, dream accounts concerning Mus'ab ibn Jaththama and Awf ibn Malik.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذه القصة قصة مصعب بن جثامة وعوف بن مالك

rows.speaker: بعض الآثار
rows.claim: Some reports say spirits may be permitted to visit their families; spirits of those who die owing prohibited loans may be detained, a restriction Al-Alusi says is not true of every debt.
rows.anchor: وربما يؤذن لأرواح بعض الناس في زيارة أهليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spirit illuminates every bodily part, even if the body is scattered; perhaps this applies to the original parts from which the person is resurrected.
rows.anchor: إن اتصال الروح بالبدن لا يختص بجزء دون جزء بل هي متصلة مشرقة على سائر أجزائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the spirit is immaterial, it has no location inside or outside the world; only the body it governs has an abode.
rows.anchor: أن الروح على القول بتجردها لا مستقر لها بل لا يقال أنها داخل العالم أو خارجه

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: Some Sufis allow one spirit to govern multiple bodies, one original and another imaginal or an extraordinary manifestation, like Gabriel appearing as Dihya or Quran as a pale man.
rows.anchor: ذكر بعضهم أن أحد البدنين هو البدن الأصلي والآخر مثالي يظهر للعيان

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: Philosophers reject one soul inhabiting multiple bodies because all the bodies would share the same knowledge; Al-Alusi says the argument also implies that any two differently informed people have different souls and proves too little.
rows.anchor: لأنه يلزم أن يكون معلوم أحدها معلوم الآخر ومجهول أحدها مجهول الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sufi theory would allow one spirit to appear in several places, as Gabriel could appear to the Prophet as Dihya without leaving the Lote Tree; they also invoke divine manifestation in forms.
rows.anchor: في حال ظهوره في صورة دحية أو أعرابي غيره بين يدي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لم يفارق سدرة المنتهى

rows.speaker: أقوال مختلفة
rows.claim: Animal spirits are said either to remain in the air after death or to cease; if animals are resurrected, Al-Alusi favors their continued existence, but if not, he favors their extinction.
rows.anchor: فالأولى أن يقال ببقاء أرواحها في الهواء أو حيث شاء الله تعالى وإن لم يكن لها حشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revealed thing that God could take away is the Quran, with its healing and mercy and the revelation by which God steadied the Prophet when opponents nearly diverted him.
rows.anchor: من القرآن الذي هو شفاء ورحمة للمؤمنين والذي ثبتناك عليه حين كادوا يفتنونك عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative expression magnifies the Quran and describes its status from the outset, showing it is not the speech of a created being.
rows.anchor: وإنما عبر عنه بالموصول تفخيما لشأنه ووصفا له بما في حيز الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first lām introduces an oath, and the following promise answers that oath rather than serving as the conditional clause; this permits omission of the object after 'if We willed'.
rows.anchor: واللام الأولى موطئة للقسم ( ولنذهبن ) جوابه النائب مناب جزاء الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking the Quran away means erasing it from manuscripts and memories, whether as written forms or stored mental images; no advocate could guarantee its restoration, and الوكيل is figurative.
rows.anchor: ويراد بالذهاب به محوه عن المصاحف والصدرور

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري وابن عطية
rows.claim: They parse except as an unrelated exception meaning 'but', correcting the prior conditional claim that God might take away the Quran.
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع على ما اختاره ابن الأنباري وابن عطية وغيرهما

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf says the exception corrects 'no advocate': after the Quran is taken away, no one could restore it, but God's mercy preserved it; this is grammatically a disconnected exception.
rows.anchor: فإن المستثنى منه ( وكيلا ) وهذا من المنقطع الممتنع إيقاعه موقع الاسم الأول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another parse makes mercy a connected exception from advocate, so mercy itself serves as the guarantor of retrieval; Al-Alusi says this strains the word advocate.
rows.anchor: اختيار أنه استثناء متصل من ( وكيلا ) أي لا تجد وكيلا باسترداده إلا الرحمة

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa parses mercy as an accusative purpose, meaning God preserved the Quran for mercy, or as an absolute object meaning God showed mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء : إن ( رحمة ) نصب على أنه مفعول له والتقدير حفظناه عليك للرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the disconnected reading, the verse favors the Prophet by preserving the Quran after favoring him with its revelation; the connected reading would make the favor only its original revelation and seems obscure.
rows.anchor: والآية على تقدير الانقطاع امتنان بإبقاء القرآن بعد الإمتنان بتنزيله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse appears to describe removal as merely hypothetical and mercy as the reason no recovery-agent would be needed, yet reports say the Quran will later be removed before the Hour.
rows.anchor: والآية ظاهرة في أن مشيئة الذهاب به غير متحققة

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: A strong report, authenticated by al-Hakim, says Islam will fade, the Quran will be lifted in one night with no verse left on earth, and only elderly people will retain the declaration of God's oneness.
rows.anchor: عن حذيفة قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : يدرس الإسلام كما يدرس وشى الثوب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن عمر
rows.claim: They report the Prophet warning against writings alongside the Quran: God may remove every Quranic letter from paper and hearts overnight, while people favored with good retain لا إله إلا الله.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وابن عمر قالا : خطب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : يا أيها الناس

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report authenticated by al-Hakim says the Quran and other revealed books will be lifted to heaven, leaving no verses or guidance in people's hearts.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال : يسري على كتاب الله تعالى فيرفع إلى السماء

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that before the Hour the Quran will return to its source, buzzing around the Throne and declaring it came from God and returns to Him, recited but not obeyed.
rows.anchor: لا تقوم الساعة حتى يرجع القرآن من حيث جاء له دوي حول العرش

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Nasr transmits a similar report attributed to Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.
rows.anchor: وأخرج محمد بن نصر نحوه مرفوعا على عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Several transmitters report Ibn Masud saying the Quran will be lifted from manuscripts and memories, after which he recited this verse; al-Bahja says removal from manuscripts comes first.
rows.anchor: وأخرج غير واحد عن ابن مسعود أنه قال : سيرفع القرآن من المصاحف والصدور ثم قرأ

rows.speaker: ابن أبي حاتم
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits that Gabriel will take the Quran away.
rows.anchor: والذاهب به هو جبريل عليه السلام كما أخرجه ابن أبي حاتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the verse predicts taking the Quran away, these reports agree with it; if it promises preservation, the conflict can be resolved by saying preservation lasts until shortly before the Hour.
rows.anchor: فإن دلت الآية على الذهاب به فلا منافاة بينها وبين هذه الأخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context signals favor: God's great favor includes revealing the Quran, choosing the Prophet above creation, making him the final prophet, and granting him the praised station.
rows.anchor: ومنه إنزال القرآن واصطفاؤه على جميع الخلق وختم الأنبياء عليهم السلام به

rows.speaker: أبو سهل
rows.claim: Abu Sahl says the verse threatens other people with losing what they received, discouraging questions about withheld knowledge such as the spirit or the Hour.
rows.anchor: إلى أنها سقيت لتهديد غيره صلى الله عليه وسلم بإذهاب ما أوتوا

rows.speaker: صاحب التحرير
rows.claim: The author of al-Tahrir suggests the delayed revelation about the spirit, Dhul-Qarnayn, and the People of the Cave distressed the Prophet, and this verse comforted him by reminding him God could remove all revelation.
rows.anchor: لما سئل عن الروح وذي القرنين وأهل الكهف وأبطأ عليه الوحي شق عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi dismisses both Abu Sahl's threat interpretation and al-Tahrir's consolation interpretation as unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: وكلا القولين كما ترى
